overview: The Safavid Empire established Twelver Shia Islam as Iran's state religion, creating the modern Iranian identity. Known for Shah Abbas I's magnificent rebuilding of Isfahan, exquisite Persian carpets, miniature painting and centuries of rivalry with the Ottoman Empire.

items.text: Shah Abbas I rebuilds Isfahan with the Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Imam Mosque and Ali Qapu Palace.
Persian carpet weaving reaches perfection, with carpets exported to European courts.
Miniature painting, calligraphy and illuminated manuscripts flourish at royal workshops.
Ismail I establishes Twelver Shia Islam as state religion, distinguishing Iran from Sunni neighbors.
Shia religious institutions, pilgrimage sites and clerical hierarchy developed.
Religious minorities including Armenians, Jews and Zoroastrians granted protected status.
Silk trade with Europe conducted through Armenian merchant networks in New Julfa.
Isfahan became one of the world's largest and most beautiful cities.
Shia Islam remains Iran's state religion to the present day.
Isfahan's architecture remains Iran's most celebrated cultural heritage.
Persian carpets and miniature paintings remain world-renowned art forms.

fall.text: Nader Shah deposed the last Safavid ruler and established the Afsharid dynasty.
